INTRAVENOUS OR MUSCULAR INJECTIONS
speechtext: Are preparations intended for intravenous or muscular administration analysed by the food and drug branch of the national health and welfare department before being released for sale to the public?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INTRAVENOUS OR MUSCULAR INJECTIONS
speechtext:
Section 13 of the Food and Drugs Act requires that samples of all batches of organic arsenicals (arsphenamine, dichlorarsphena-mine hydrochloride, neoarsphenamine, oxo-phenarsine hydrochloride and sulpharsphena-mine) be not distributed until the Minister of National Health and Welfare has indicated
that each batch is not unsafe for use. Each batch is analysed or biologically tested before being released for sale.
In addition, parenteral products controlled under section 12 of the act may not be sold until the minister is satisfied that the premises, in which the drugs mentioned in schedules C and D of the act are manufactured, are suitable and that the processes and conditions of manufacture are satisfactory to produce drugs that are safe when properly used. Schedules C and D include insulin, vaccines, sera and antibiotics.
Factories manufacturing these products are carefully inspected and samples are tested from time to time. Several batches of any new products added to any manufacturer's list are tested before being released for sale to make sure they are safe and samples are taken at intervals thereafter for test.
All other parenteral drugs are spot checked for safety and identity. Conditions under which these drugs are manufactured are also being checked by the food and drug inspectors.

That is the point at issue between the hon. member and myself. He has of course the right to discuss this answer which, in his view, is not satisfactory, but he is discussing it at the wrong time. speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):

Inquiries of the Ministry to questions in the same form, but that now he is denied similar information.
Since it appears that we are becoming increasingly bound by precedent, I do not think a precedent of this nature should be established by simply ignoring what would occur if this were allowed to pass. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FIRMS PAID TO ACT AS DISTRIBUTORS

speechtext: Since the point has been raised, might I point out that what I was directing my remarks to was not the question of whether it was evasive. I immediately concede that that is debatable. What I am pointing out is that the hon. member has said that the question sought information which had been given in reply to similar questions in earlier years. Now he is confronted with the answer that this information will not be given. That, Mr. Speaker, suddenly changes the procedure which has been accepted and followed. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FIRMS PAID TO ACT AS DISTRIBUTORS

that, as far as I am personally concerned at this moment, there is not much else I can do.
The point may be more complicated than I can perceive at the moment. I shall look into the remarks of the hon. member and also the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition, and if need be I shall clarify or modify the remarks I have made. Generally speaking, questions asked on the orders of the day are to be brief and of an urgent and national character. Whatever answers ministers feel free to give must be accepted as the answers. Even on questions on the order paper, if the minister says "No, I cannot answer this question", the question is answered.
On earlier occasions I have given the precedents with respect to that, and if necessary I shall give them again. But the particular point that has been raised by the hon. member, by way of complaining about the return received, which he feels is not complete-well, that is a different matter. I shall go into it further, and if necessary I shall give a ruling on it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FIRMS PAID TO ACT AS DISTRIBUTORS
speechtext:
With respect to the point raised earlier by the hon. member for Peterborough and pursued by the Leader of the Opposition, I should like to refer them to citation 137 of Beauchesne's third edition, which appears at page 67 and reads as follows:
When the orders of the day are called by the Speaker and before they are read by the Clerk Assistant, it is the practice sanctioned by usage but not by any positive rule for members to make personal explanations or ask questions of the government in reference to . . .
Then down approximately at the middle of that citation I read the appropriate section:
. . . or in respect to delay in obtaining returns or to the incompleteness of certain returns brought down under the order of the house; . . .
And so on. I think that is part of the case with which we were faced today. If hon. members look further in the same edition at citation 307, they will see the following:
A minister may decline to answer a question without stating the reason for his refusal, and insistence on an answer is out of order, no debate being allowed. A refusal to answer cannot be raised as a question of privilege, nor is it regular to comment upon such refusal. A member can put a question, but has no right to insist upon an answer.

It would seem desirable at the same time to prevent money accumulating in the fund if for any reason the normal rate of activity in grade crossing projects remained below the available resources in the fund.

Until parliament enacts otherwise there should be an appropriation of $5 million instead of the present $1 million, to the fund each year from April 1, 1954, with a proviso that where on April 1st in any such year there is an uncommitted balance of more than $2 million in the fund the appropriation for that year should be such sum as with the uncommitted balance will amount to $7 million.

There were 65 on the list at that time, 11 of which were urban and were considered of major importance, the remainder being rural. With such a program in front of them it would not seem that the limitation would have any effect for probably four, five or six years, and therefore there would not seem to be any particular reason for pressing the point. I think the operations under the fund will use up the $5 million every year, and it will not be necessary to put the $7 million restriction into effect.

Then there is the question of maintenance. The board recommended that a $200 limit be established on contributions from the fund for the maintenance of any particular protected crossing. Recommendation No. 4 on page 116 of the report is as follows:
Contributions should be permitted towards the annual cost of maintenance and operation of automatic signals installed at crossings after the amendment comes into force, the contribution in respect of any one crossing not to exceed for any year the actual cost for that year nor exceed $200.
As a result of its investigations the board was of the opinion that some consideration should be given to the maintenance of grade level crossings where protective devices had been installed. But for some reason or other, possibly because it was too expensive, the government decided that such maintenance was not necessary. To give the committee some idea of what the board thought about the matter I should like to read the following from page 72 of their report:
At the same time the maintenance of roads and streets under municipal control has been growing more onerous. Without revenues derived from the automobile industry or highway traffic, the municipalities have acquired heavy new responsibilities which, unless outside assistance is obtained, must be met from their general tax rates . . . Such costs of construction and maintenance of municipal roads and streets are a substantial burden on the municipalities.
They go on further to point out, as was mentioned in the debate, that the average maintenance cost per year for rural crossings was $560 and for urban crossings $865. Therefore an amount of $200 for each protected crossing would not seem to be out of place. However, as the years go by the amount will pile up, and I suppose the government in its wisdom thought it would be a good thing not to act upon this recommendation at the present time. But the municipalities are the ones who are going to have to bear the burden, and they are not going to be helped to any extent. Their situation is set out quite effectively in the last paragraph I read from the report. At page 100 of the report the board went on to say:
Because of the fact that the assumption of a share of the annual maintenance costs by the fund would create a continuing liability, we believe that any steps in this direction should be most carefully considered.
I presume that is the reason for the government's action. The report goes on to say:
Nevertheless we feel that the cost of maintenance has been and will undoubtedly be increasingly a deterrent to grade crossing protection projects, particularly where small or financially weak municipalities are concerned. An expenditure for a capital improvement requires to be voted but once, and can be undertaken when the means are seen to he available. Maintenance expenditure, however, is in the nature of an overhead or fixed cost which may increase as general costs increase and cannot be amortized. For some municipalities

Railway Act
it may be entirely out of the question to pledge future tax revenues in this way. The railways position is similar.
I believe the government should give consideration to this charge upon the municipalities because, as has been pointed out all through the board's report, the burden of meeting the cost is quite heavy and that is the reason the municipalities want assistance. We went along with the increase in the fund from $1 million to $5 million, though we thought it should have been considerably extended so as to cover the maintenance of protected crossings. I believe the government should make a concession there and allow something to help relieve the burden imposed upon municipalities. At page 101 of the report the board goes on to say:
For these reasons, it would seem in order that the fund assume some share of the maintenance costs, since a good proportion of these wili be incurred as a result of the proposed extended a d to new projects in the coming years. We wouW recommend that a fixed amount of $200 be tne contribution from the fund toward annual mam-tenance and operation charges only on automatic lig "is installed at crossings after the date this provision takes effect.
From the language used by the board it is apparent they were quite confident the government would adopt their recommendation. I continue:
Where maintenance of such in:^^the^otal the amount contributed would be only the total amount actually spent on maintenance. The re Tainins maintenance costs would be apportioned "ccordmg to principles already laid down or previous practices of the board.
Notwithstanding that the committee has not seen fit to implement that recommendation I think it would be wise for the government to at least take another look at the matter and reconsider its attitude because on its own admission it is going to be a burden upon the municipalities. I do not think it would put too great a strain on the fund if a contribution of $200 for maintenance were granted. On principle the municipalities are entitled to some consideration.
I come now to the point which I consider the most important. It has to do with the rules and regulations for the protection of the public at level crossings. This subject covers a very wide field, including not only transportation but also industry. There are accident prevention associations to protect workers, notwithstanding that the workers may be indifferent and do not feel that the rules are necessary. Nevertheless the mounting accident toll in industry is such that precautions have to be taken to do something even for people who do not want anything done for them. In other words, after .a fatality has occurred in an industry, on the
fMr. Small.]
highway or at a grade level! crossing,, the burden falls upon the taxpayers- It is not only the persons killed or injured who; suffer; their families suffer also. Therefore all regulations tha-t are laid down for the prevention of accidents have more in mind the protection of the families and the resulting drain upon some treasury or other.
When the question was before the committee even the railways recognized; its; importance, and the fact that something should be done to see that the regulations were enforced. They asked that some penalty be imposed upon those who disregard signals at grade level crossings. Devices are installed at crossings for the protection of the public and a lot of money is spent for that purpose, but then we do not take any measures to see that the signals are observed. In fact there is no penalty to make- people observe them. It would be helpful, even if the- penalty were only small.
The railways also emphasized the effect on the morale of their engineers and firemen who are involved in accidents. They can see the accident is going to happen, and they cannot do anything to stop it. The railways claim it has a devastating effect on their operators, and therefore the people using the highways and level crossings should be made to realize they must observe the warning signs. A request was made that teeth be put into the regulation by the imposition of a $25 fine, and I feel that is a good suggestion. I believe the government should give some consideration to. implementing that recommendation made by the Canadian National.
I could go further and emphasize the portions of the report dealing with observance of the regulations. Mention is made on page 45 of the advance warning signs which are a matter of provincial and municipal responsibility. The report reads:
As to the advance warning signs to be used, this is a matter for which the provinces and municipalities are primarily responsible. Under today's traffic conditions they are almost indispensable but the board has no authority to require the erection of such signs by the provinces or municipalities and the applicability of the fund limited to improvements at crossings.
This is a matter that concerns the railways, and I feel that we should be sufficiently interested to see that some form of assistance is given or some means found to enforce upon the people using the highways the observance of these signs. An accident is not always the railway's fault. Then on page 107 of the report we find this:
Nevertheless the widespread concern with the problem of reducing or preventing grade crossing accidents is ample justification for the establishment of informal advisory committees. For the

time being, these should be on a provincial basis. Apart from the difficulties of working through a large national body, provincially organized committees would permit a great deal of the necessary preliminary work to be done more expeditiously. By this means, municipal and other representatives would become more quickly conversant with the general aspect of the problem and the particular needs within their own province and what actions could be undertaken to meet these needs.
I believe that part oi the report is particularly applicable at the present time. In the future there will be dominion-provincial conferences at which this matter can be considered. It is a matter of public relations and the education of the public. The thing that brought this to my attention was the receipt in the mail the other day of the program for a national highway safety conference to be held in Ottawa from May 24 to May 26. Would it not be a fine move on the part of this government if such legislation were enacted, or some tacit understanding given that this legislation would contain a clause providing a penalty for disregarding railway signs. The good roads association is sponsoring this safety conference, and many other organizations are greatly interested in it. The fact that a conference is being called is, I believe, a good sign.
The program for the fourth plenary session of this conference mentions reports of delegate divisions on proposals for implementing a Canadian highway safety program and recommendations for continuation of the national highway safety conference. These organizations are greatly concerned, because highway safety vitally affects them. I believe the fact that there are public bodies so much concerned about this that they would like to have something done about it is a good start.
I am not criticizing the minister because nothing has been done. Everyone seems to have the same attitude toward the prevention of accidents. It is all right as long as it does not cost any money or cause any trouble. As soon as you enter the realm of a financial undertaking, then they more or less try to evade any responsibility. This program for the national highway safety conference is a good start. Probably the minister would be in accord with the aims of that conference. If the sponsors of the conference were smart they would have the minister there to address them.
In view of the fact that a start has been made on the establishment of a committee on a national basis I believe the government would be well advised, through the transport commission, to enter into some kind of arrangement with them as to the best means
Railway Act
of implementing legislation that would give effect to these regulations concerning level crossings.
Those are my general comments on the deficiencies of this bill as it has been presented to the house. We are not critical of the government's proposition, but we feel a vast improvement could be made if some consideration were given to the three points I have mentioned.

On several occasions, Mr. Chairman, I have made comments on this bill. I do not wish to go over any of the material that was discussed earlier, but I do feel that the evidence given before the committee indicates the need for further action toward the elimination of level crossings in Canada. I do feel that the evidence submitted by both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National indicates the need for greater emphasis on grade separation projects.
In the committee the Canadian Pacific representative gave us a table showing maintenance and operation costs of railway crossing protection devices during the year 1954. When one considers the relatively high expenditure each year on the maintenance and operation of these protective devices, one must consider just what we get for the dollar that is invested in those types of safety devices.
The report of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada has given us information concerning the number of accidents at crossings protected by automatic signal devices. We do know that in a seven-year period the accident frequency at crossings protected by automatic devices was 4-9 per year per hundred crossings. There was an accident frequency of 1-2 accidents per year per hundred unprotected crossings. It would seem that even though we spent money and the railway companies spent money on the construction and maintenance of automatic signal devices, they have not been altogether effective in reducing the accidents. We know there is a heavier flow of traffic across these protected crossings, but we have to consider the amount of money we are spending to protect these crossings. When we consider that in the light of the number of accidents I think it is quite obvious that we might be further ahead, from the economic standpoint, if we laid greater stress on grade separation projects.
In the committee I asked the Canadian National engineering expert about the life span of a subway, and he replied that it was something in the neighbourhood of 75 years. The maintenance cost of subways is relatively low, particularly in the earlier years. I hope

Railway Act
the government does not feel that this problem is solved with the passage of this bill or that it has discharged its obligations in connection with level crossing protection in Canada. I feel that the type of information we received in committee points to the fact that this is merely a start, and hope the government will pursue this matter and next session will go further toward the elimination of level crossings, particuarly through grade separation projects. The hon. member for Danforth mentioned one matter that was discussed at some length in committee, having to do with safety devices at level crossings. It is one thing to build a protective device of some kind but it is quite another thing, of course, to have people pay attention to it. The representative of the Canadian National Railways was quite concerned about the fact that even if the railway company did erect protective devices, many of the travelling public would ignore them; and perhaps to some extent that is why we have a relatively high accident rate at protected level crossings.
The Canadian National Railways were most anxious that parliament should amend the Railway Act to make it a criminal offence for the driver of a motor vehicle to cross at a protected crossing when a signal is in operation. Since the subject has been raised by the hon. member for Danforth, while there might be some question from a constitutional standpoint as to the competence of parliament to amend the Railway Act to cover the matter in question, I would point out that in my own province of Saskatchewan we have in our vehicles act the very provision which I believe the railways are anxious to have placed in the federal legislation.
Section 134 of our vehicles act in the province states, in part, as follows:
(2)	The driver of a vehicle approaching a level railway crossing shall, when any signalman, any automatic signal or other safety device indicates the approach of a train, bring the vehicle to a dead stop, and shall not proceed until the signalman, automatic signal or device indicates that it is safe to do so.
(3)	The driver of a vehicle shall, before proceeding over a level railway crossing on the approach to which a sign indicating danger, or stop sign, is erected, whether or not a train can be seen or heard approaching the crossing, bring his vehicle to a dead stop at the danger or stop sign and shall not proceed until it is safe to do so.
As was pointed out by the representative of the Canadian National Railways, and from what I have learned in conversation with friends of mine who are railway engineers, perhaps the toughest part of an engineer's job, when approaching a level crossing, is

when he sees a car approaching and does not know until the very last second whether the car is going to stop, or whether the driver will be so rash as to try to cross the tracks before the train reaches the crossing. Not only would we be doing something to eliminate accidents, we would be making railway engineers much happier if we were to have a uniform provision of the kind I have indicated.
Since in committee we did not decide whether the provincial or the federal government was competent to deal with the matter, I would ask the minister to make an investigation to learn whether it is possible to make such amendment to the Railway Act, perhaps following in form the act we have in Saskatchewan.
I believe this bill is good, as far as it goes. There can be no doubt that the increase to $5 million meets with the approval of all hon. members. However, I do not want the minister or the government to feel that the acceptance of this measure deals with the problem completely. In my view this measure only scratches the surface. While we support the bill wholeheartedly, I am hoping that at some future time the minister will And it possible to bring forward legislation to extend this principle.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to thank the hon. member for New Westminster for allowing me to speak in his place at this time. This afternoon I shall place before the committee an example of a grade crossing which, right today, illustrates in a practical fashion the weaknesses in both principle and detail to be found in Bill 259, now before us. While my observation will be directed to the first clause in the bill, I shall have some comment to make concerning other clauses.
In advance of making any comment, I think it might be well to place before the committee certain facts to show the relationship between the measure before us and the circumstances I shall set out. Apparently after consultation between the board of transport commissioners and the Canadian National Railways a decision was reached to make certain changes at a grade crossing in the town of Ingersoll, Ontario. The crossing in question is where the Canadian National Railways main line intersects provincial highway No. 2. Hon. members are no doubt aware of the fact that provincial highway No. 2 in Ontario is perhaps one of the busiest, if not the busiest, in the province, serving as the main link between Windsor and Montreal.

There is of course a great deal of traffic over this highway. Much of this is in the form of transport and truck vehicles, but there is also a large amount of tourist traffic in the summer months. In the past this crossing in Ingersoll has presented a great traffic hazard and has been the cause of many traffic jams. Some days it takes more than half an hour to make the crossing at this point.
I appreciate that in the past there has been some considerable difficulty. However, at the present time the highways program in Ontario is making headway, with the result that a new highway known as No. 401 is under construction, running parallel to highway No. 2 which, it is expected, eventually will take the place of that highway. I believe a portion of the new construction will be open for use this fall, by-passing the cities of London and Woodstock and the town of Ingersoll. I have taken some time to state the background, because it has a bearing on what I shall say later.
It appears that in the past this level crossing has been altered several times, and contributions to that end have been made from the fund. I shall not waste the time of the committee by stating details in this connection. However, I should like to read some paragraphs from correspondence which has taken place concerning this crossing, and which I believe tell the story very well. I would refer first to a portion of a letter dated May 2, 1955, from what appears to be the legal department of the Canadian National Railways. There is some uncertainty in my mind concerning the signature on the letter, and it occurs to me that the person here named may also be legal counsel for the board of transport commissioners. Perhaps the minister will enlighten us on this point.
This letter is addressed to E. R. Hopkins, secretary of the board of transport commissioners. It bears the file number 5087 and refers to "Protection at Thames street, Ingersoll, Ontario". The letter says, in part:
With reference to your letter of February 17 last concerning protection at the above crossing, wherein, after an inspection by the board's engineer it was recommended that electric lights be installed on each of the present gate arms with a stand-by battery-
Then it proceeds to refer to previous improvements made at the crossing. At a later point the letter states:
Conditions at this crossing are much more favourable and it is recommended that automatically controlled short arm gates with flashing light signals and bell be installed in lieu of the present mechanical gate as shown on drawing-

Then follow certain letters and figures identifying the drawings to which reference is made. It continues:
Also enclosed herewith is detailed estimate showing the cost to be approximately $17,350 with an estimated annual maintenance cost of $825.
It is considered that this type of protection constitutes an improvement made desirable by increased highway traffic, and it is therefore submitted that a contribution of 40 per cent of the cost be made from the railway grade crossing fund and the balance of the installation costs be assessed equally between the town and the railway company. It is further submitted that the cost of maintenance be shared equally by the municipality and the railway company.
I should now like to refer to a letter which was sent to the secretary of the board of transport commissioners by the solicitors for the town of Ingersoll, dated May 12, 1955. The pertinent part of the letter reads as follows:
The municipal council of the corporation of the town of Ingersoll have carefully perused the proposed undertaking and they wish to object to such undertaking on the grounds that the share of the expenses allotted to the corporation of the town of Ingersoll on its 30 per cent basis would appear to be $5,205 and it would also appear that the annual maintenance cost of same to the town of Ingersoll would be $412.50 according to the proposal submitted to the board of transport commissioners.
The town of Ingersoll is of the opinion that the protection given this crossing in the past by way of gates has been satisfactory; also the new super highway No. 401 which will pass within one mile south of Ingersoll when it is opened in about a year's time will considerably diminish the traffic which now passes through our town on Queens highway No. 2.
May this letter be deemed a formal protest on behalf of the corporation of the town of Ingersoll to such an undertaking.
I wish to refer to a third letter. It is addressed to myself by the solicitors, Messrs. Start and Marshall, of the town of Ingersoll. The pertinent part reads:
Dear Mr. Nesbitt:
We are enclosing herewith a copy of the letter received by the town as an enclosure from the Canadian National Railways to the board of transport commissioners. We are also enclosing herewith a copy of our letter to the board objecting to this undertaking by the town in view of the cost of same to the town. The total estimated cost of installation is $17,350 and it is proposed that this be paid for as follows:
Share from grade crossing fund-40 per cent, $6,940.
Canadian National Railways share-30 per cent, $5,205.
Town's share-30 per cent. $5,205.
It is estimated also that the annual maintenance cost will be $825, and this will be assumed equally by the railroad and the town approximating $412.50 each annually.
Here is the situation, Mr. Chairman. I imagine the minister has never heard of a situation like this before. The municipality is objecting to the improvement in protection of the grade crossing. This must be the one case

Railway Act
in a thousand, but it exists nevertheless. This town does not want it for three reasons. The first is because of the cost allocation; second, the maintenance allocation; and third, it is entirely unnecessary because when the new highway is opened in the fall there will not be any traffic problem on this railway crossing since the traffic, which is the main objection and the main cause of trouble at the crossing now, will be very largely eliminated by the opening of a new highway.
The comments I should like to make are as follows. First of all there is the apportionment of costs. When Bill No. 259 is passed the apportionment will be 60 per cent to the grade crossing fund, 25 per cent to the railway, and 15 per cent to the municipality. Yet this letter indicates that the cost will be on the old basis of 40 per cent, 30 per cent and 30 per cent. This will make a very considerable difference. If this crossing protection is proceeded with against the wishes of the town of Ingersoll, at least it should be made very clear to the town that the apportionment will be on the new basis and not on the old. I do not believe any orders have yet been given.
This is a situation that will come up in a number of cases where it had been decided to build these crossings before the passage of the present bill. The minister might give us some assurance that any of these grade crossings that are contemplated and have been authorized at the present time will have their costs apportioned on the basis of the amendments to the act before us at the present time. I say that because it would make the following difference in this case.
If the apportionment as suggested in the present amendments were used, the grade crossing fund would have to pay $10,410 instead of $6,940. The railway's share would be $4,337.50 instead of $5,205, and the town of Ingersoll's share would be $2,602.50 instead of $5,205. I hope when the minister makes his remarks later on he will be able to give us some assurance on this point.
There is one other matter in connection with the apportionment that I am a little curious about. It has to do with clause 265 (2) (b), which reads as follows:
In the case of reconstruction and improvement of a grade separation at a crossing, 30 per cent of such cost or $150,000, whichever is the lesser.
In the particular instance to which I am referring no grade separation is contemplated. It is merely a change in protective devices. It is not a grade separation. However, it is not quite clear to me why in the case of reconstruction and improvement of a grade separation the fund can provide only 30 per cent instead of 60 per cent, as is proposed in

this bill, or 40 per cent, as was done before.
I do not quite understand the principle behind that. I hope we may receive some enlightenment later on.
The question of provision for maintenance has been mentioned by the hon. member for Danforth. Bill No. 259 does not contain any provision for maintenance of those grade crossings out of the fund. As has already been mentioned, apparently this has been recommended to the government by the board of transport commissioners. It can be said that this provision for maintenance was not put in the bill, but it is hoped that the bill may be amended so the board can make certain allowances in some instances, because a great many of these municipalities, particularly the small ones, are heavily overburdened with taxes. Every hon. member knows that, and there is no need for me to go into the matter any farther. As I look at this bill I still think the government might improve it a little and provide for the maintenance of the grade crossings out of the fund.
The last thing I should like to mention has puzzled me a little in the past few days, and also other hon. members. I am wondering how the federal parliament by an act, namely the Railway Act, can force municipalities to pay for the construction and maintenance of grade crossings against their will. Such legislation, on the face of it at least, seems to be ultra vires, since it is an invasion of property and civil rights, specifically reserved to the provinces.
However, I believe two similar cases have gone to the privy council, which have decided the matter. The first case was that of Toronto v. the Canadian Pacific Railway, reported in 1908 Appeal Cases, page 54. The other case was that of Toronto Railway v. City of Toronto, 1920 Appeal Cases, page 426. I might say a summary of the judgments in these cases was that legislation by parliament imposing, in effect, charges upon persons benefiting from railway improvements to provide for the expenses of such improvements was upheld. The provisions, challenged because they imposed burdens on persons peculiarly within the jurisdiction of the province, were held, nevertheless, to be intra vires as being ancillary to the main purpose.
I do not think the question arises in this case of whether or not municipalities are emanations of the crown in the right of the province because I think that is clearly not the situation. Municipalities are clearly persons created by the provinces. Perhaps the minister might agree with the point that if

the provincial governments, who are in control of provincial highways, were ordered by the board to contribute to the cost of construction of grade crossings, the provincial governments would be perfectly within their rights' to refuse to do so. However, I would be interested to hear any comments the minister would care to make in that regard.
The two cases I refer to were not exactly in point with respect to grade crossings. Even on general principles the privy council and other courts in Canada have frequently distinguished on the facts. I am not entirely satisfied yet that this legislation is not ultra vires.
I should like to suggest one or two thoughts to the minister and I would be interested, as I said before, to hear his comments. The questions that arise in my mind are, first, are grade crossings for the sole benefit of the municipality in which they are constructed? In many cases are not adjacent municipalities benefited, and should they not be assessed? How about provincial highways? The particular situation at Ingersoll to which I have just referred is not a matter of local traffic at all. The traffic here is mainly through provincial traffic from centres such as Toronto to London and Windsor. Those centres are benefited far more than the town of Ingersoll, which is being assessed. I think allowance should be made for this, if not at this time then in future legislation. In any event it seems to me unfair.
I know the principle has been recognized that the municipality should pay a certain portion of the cost of these grade crossings. It seems to me unfair that the municipality should be asked to pay anything. I know it will be said that the municipality benefits from the grade crossing. This is quite true, but I submit that the railroad and the grade crossing fund should bear the whole cost.
First of all there is a practical reason for this. The federal government provides funds for the railways, at least for the Canadian National Railways, and for the grade crossing fund. The federal government has greater means of raising revenue. As everyone knows, the municipalities have only limited means of raising taxation, and they are already overburdened with education and local road costs. It does not seem exactly logical or reasonable that the municipalities should be forced to help pay for the construction of grade crossings.
It is true that there is benefit to the municipality, but we must remember that the problem is created by the fact that the railroad is there. If there were no railroad there would be no need for a grade crossing 50433-246
Railway Act
and there would be no traffic problem at that particular point. I know it is certainly said that the municipalities benefit from the railways, which is quite true, but that should be considered more on a national basis. I believe consideration should be given, if not at this time then in the future, to further reduce if not extinguish completely the amount the municipalities have to pay.
I recognize that the government has considered the matter, and also that under the new apportionment of costs the municipality will pay must less than it had to pay before. We all appreciate this, but I think it should be carried a little further. After all, it is the position of the railroad tracks which creates the traffic problem.
I think I have said all I wish to say on this matter, but I shall conclude with one observation. The town of Ingersoll in the county of Oxford does not want this improved grade crossing protection, but I can assure the minister that the citizens of that county would be most grateful if the board of transport commissioners would divert their attention from Ingersoll to the Creditville crossing, seven miles east of Woodstock, where a grade crossing is badly needed.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill was considered at length in committee, and it is unfortunate that the report of the committee is not available so hon. members could be thoroughly acquainted with what was said during the discussion of the bill and its various aspects. It may be necessary to repeat what took place at that time, and thus some of the work already done will be lost.
We in this group support the main spirit of the bill, that is that additional funds be made available for the elimination of grade crossings. I think that is the general spirit in which everyone accepts the tenor of the bill. However, as I pointed out in the committee, this bill is not a complete answer to railway crossing deaths. It will help materially to cut down the number of accidents, but we are going to have accidents at railway crossings whether we have overpasses or underpasses and spend millions of dollars in erecting various types of signals.
There are other factors to be taken into consideration, more particularly the lack of caution on the part of many motorists. The automatic signals we have today definitely are not the answer, nor is the overpass or the underpass. People deliberately commit suicide by means of excessive speed, because they freeze at the wheels of their cars, and because of other human factors. Then there are the mechanical factors to be considered, as well as weather and other conditions. While this

Railway Act
$5 million we are setting aside for the grade crossing fund will be of material benefit, we cannot look forward to it cutting out all accidents.
The hon. member for Oxford during his remarks indicated that he felt there was a constitutional question involved in this first clause, under which the board is to fix the share of the cost to be paid by the municipal district. I agree with him in that respect. The hon. member cited two cases in which there was some question of illegality, but it is not established in my mind that this bill authorizing the board to apportion a share of the cost to the municipal district is completely intra vires.
The municipality is a creature of the provincial government and has authority vested in it as such. We are dealing here with a board which receives its authority by federal right. I question very much the right of any board constituted under federal authority to exercise this power on a municipal district which receives its power by act of a provincial authority.
We should examine this very closely. As is indicated, the town of Ingersoll, which the hon. member mentioned, seems to feel the same way about it. It does not want this particular overpass or underpass, which would indicate that it should not be forced upon the town unless it agrees to it.
On examining the bill further I notice that no provision is made for the construction of overpasses or underpasses in connection with new roads. I cannot understand the reason for this, because in the building of new highways, such as the provincial governments are building today, at times it would be better to spend a few thousand dollars extra in order to build a road along a route where it might be possible to use a natural underpass or overpass, as the case might be, whereas at the present time under the present system whereby no money is set aside to assist in the building of such a crossing, the provincial authority would take the easier route for the road and say, "Well, it is simpler; we will save a couple of hundred thousand dollars or a few thousand dollars". But that saving in itself would not be sufficient to build the overhead pass or the underpass.
I think something should have been set aside in the bill that made it possible to contribute something to it, and that is not included. We feel that the provincial government possibly, the federal authorities, the municipal governments and the railways should bear the cost of these crossings to a lesser or greater degree, depending upon the

location and other factors and that a fixed sum should not be set aside for municipal participation.
There are certain factors that we require educating in. For instance, we need uniform road signs leading to railway crossings. There is no such thing in the dominion. I would suggest that possibly a certain part of this sum should be set aside for that purpose, in order to discuss and to discover the feasibility and the possibility of having a national system of road signs wherever there are crossings.
Then we should have a uniform law that might be passed in respect to approaches to railway crossings. X think the hon. member for Regina City mentioned this too. The province of Saskatchewan has some enabling legislation, I believe, and the province of British Columbia has legislation governing this matter. But there are in Canada provinces which do not have any such regulations. I would say that we would be well advised to see if it would not be possible to incorporate within our act, through agreements with the provincial governments, provision that there should be uniformity of regulation pertaining to speed and other factors, road signals and on roads leading to crossings.
As to motor vehicles approaching railway crossings, in the table that was given us in committee by the Canadian Pacific Railway I find they have, for instance, eight different types of protective signals.
People who come from other parts of Canada are not too familiar with all of these types. I can well remember in the early thirties when, in making a trip through the southern part of the United States, I came to the city of Reno. It is true that I happened to note this wigwag affair but I had never seen one before. I did not know what it was there for.
I had seen no railway sign such as we have here in Canada at this place. You can imagine my amazement when a train sped before the car at that moment.
That is an indication of the type of thing with respect to which I feel we should try to gain uniformity in this country.
Among the various types of protection that have been set aside by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and apparently approved by the board are automatic bells, automatic danger signals, automatic wigwags, automatic flashing lights, automatic gates, manual mechanical gates, manual electric gates, and manual flashing lights. The numbers of them range from four in the case of the automatic bell to 270 in the case of the automatic flashing light. I know that we have uniform railway crossing signs at or before we reach

each of the crossings, possibly. But this white and black sign may not be efficient. It certainly does not appear to be sufficient or we would not have as many accidents at railway crossings as we have at the present time. For that reason I think it would be important that we should set aside part of this fund to make it necessary to have one uniform type of indicator to let the people know when they are approaching an automatic signal at a railway crossing or one that might be even manually operated. Certainly we should not have as many as eight different kinds.
In order to assist further in this matter I would also propose that we should set aside possibly a sum equal to what we have here for this railway crossing fund in this bill for the purpose of educating our high school students in the proper way of driving, the recognition of signals, and the traffic laws as they exist in the country.

Mr. Chairman, after all this flattery from my friend from Fort William, I scarcely know what to say. I believe we always try to carry on our discussions thoroughly in that committee.
For many years the question of grade crossings has aroused keen interest in the House of Commons, and it was as a result of that interest that the board of transport commissioners was requested to investigate the whole problem of railway grade crossings and to bring in a report. Hon. members know that the report was brought in about a year ago; in fact, to be specific, it is dated May 10, 1954. The legislation we are now considering follows that report.
I suggest we should bear that in mind, because the result is that the measure now before us is unlikely to be amended in the near future. It is presented as a result of the report, and in another year, or perhaps two or three years, there will not be the authority of a report behind any amendments which may be introduced by the government. For that reason I think we should be careful to see that the bill we are now passing is complete.

There was a clear recommendation from the board of transport commissioners on that point. I refer of course to paragraph 4 of the recommendations which is in these words:
Contributions should be permitted towards the annual cost of maintenance and operation of automatic signals installed at crossings after the amendment comes into force

That applies to installations made from now on. It continues:
-the contribution in respect of any one crossing not to exceed for any year the actual cost for that year nor exceed $200.

He pointed out that all the money should be used for new grade separations, or for improvements to old ones, and that no moneys should be set aside for costs of maintenance and operation. Then he added this, as it appears at page 2135 of Hansard:
Perhaps I should add that if we become convinced at some future date that this would be a useful addition to the powers of the board in respect to the fund we would be quite prepared to consider it.
The evidence we got in committee from the railways on this point was very clear. The Canadian Pacific Railway filed a table showing that in 1954 the cost to them of maintaining and operating highway crossing protection devices was $452,033.

subtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That was not for maintenance alone, was it?

subtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: The amount for maintenance was $179,227 and that for operation was $272,805, making the total of $452,033 I have mentioned.

subtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I think that amount included sums paid to operators of manual protection devices, did it not?

subtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
My understanding is that this was the total cost to them of maintaining and operating these highway crossing protection devices. And, mind you, they were not paying the total cost, because a proportion of that cost was paid by the municipalities, except in the case of automatic danger signs where the railways paid 100 per cent. In connection with automatic bells they paid 80 per cent; for automatic wigwags, 62-5 per
Railway Act
cent; for automatic flashing lights, 52-8 per cent; for automatic gates, 66-2 per cent; for manual mechanical gates, 64-7 per cent; for manual electric gates 65 [DOT] 0 per cent and for manual flashing lights, 61-1 per cent. The difference was paid by one municipality or another or, in certain cases, possibly by a province.
These costs represent the costs of protecting level crossings, and are costs just in the same way as the amounts paid for grade separation projects. I cannot see why some assistance should not be made available from the grade crossing fund.
One result of the failure to give help in maintaining and operating these devices is that the municipalities will hesitate to make application for warning devices. The hon. member for Oxford has given a very good example today, when he tells us that the town of Ingersoll does not believe it should have to pay half the cost of maintaining and operating certain safety devices. I cannot understand why the minister and his department failed to implement that particular recommendation in the legislation that we are considering this afternoon.
The other point which I believe should have been included in the bill was based on a request made by the Canadian National Railways. Mind you, the Canadian National Railways have never been very forward in making suggestions about legislation to the committee. In most cases the Canadian Pacific Railway has to do the leading in requesting changes and, of course, the Canadian National Railways benefit by whatever changes the Canadian Pacific Railway can bring about as a result of the representations. But in this particular instance, the representative of the Canadian National Railways made a very clear-cut recommendation to the standing committee. He pointed out that there is no penalty clause in the railway act under which a person who has failed to pay attention to a safety device installed on the order of the board can be prosecuted. In other words, he was not referring to devices which have just been installed by the railway without an order, but to devices that the board of transport commissioners have ordered installed. He said that attempts had been made to prosecute people under the reckless driving provision of the code, but without success. The Canadian National Railways found itself unable to take adequate proceedings against a person who failed to heed those safety devices. He recommended that there should be a subsection written

Railway Act
into the Railway Act. It would be subsection 2 of section 416, and would read as follows:
Any person who, in using any highway crossing at rail level for the purpose of passing on foot-
It has wider application than over a motor vehicle; it applies also to foot traffic. I continue with the proposed subsection:
-or in any vehicle along such highway across the railway, disregards signs, signals, or other protective devices erected or otherwise provided by the company pursuant to order of the board, is liable, on summary conviction, to a penalty not exceeding $25.
The first clause of section 416 provides a penalty for a person who walks across a railway instead of going over a foot bridge, where there is a foot bridge in existence. I do not think there can be any doubt that if clause 1 is within the jurisdiction of the dominion parliament, the proposed clause 2 would also be intra vires.
The representative of the railway said that if this provision were written into the law he believed it would help to cut down the number of accidents. I believe there was considerable support in the committee for this submission but the minister declined to accept such an amendment and of course it was not written into the act.
The final disposition of the proposal was that the minister would write to the different provincial governments asking them if they had any objection to there being a provision of the kind suggested written into the Railway Act. I do not intend to go any farther with this matter today, but I urge upon the minister once more that he accept this recommendation which was made by the Canadian National Railways and was supported by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
None of us likes to see more penalty clauses written into legislation. There are, of course, many, many penalty clauses of all kinds facing every Canadian every minute of the day that he or she is awake; but here is a suggestion which fits in with the purposes of the grade crossing fund, namely, to cut down accidents at level crossings. I do submit that the suggestion could very well be accepted by the minister and the government.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I want to answer the suggestions of the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne). He spoke at some length about the situation in Quebec city, which is known to me, as I have often travelled by rail to Quebec. But I must say that in order to

improve the existing situation in his city, it would be best to vote in favour of the measure which is now under consideration.
This legislation will put at the disposal of the municipalities willing to undertake projects of this kind-which are needed in the city of Quebec-much more considerable amounts than the latter was able to get under the act now being amended.
(Text):
I should like to try to deal summarily with the principal matters which have been raised during the discussions this afternoon. I think the first and perhaps the most important point mentioned is the increasing of the annual contribution from $1 million to $5 million. I think there has been in the minds of several members of the committee the thought that it would have been desirable to have provided a larger sum than $5 million. In that connection I should like to quote a paragraph from the report of the board of transport commissioners, which will be found on page 59 of the printed report, in which they say:
It is our considered opinion that a program of these proportions would represent the maximum amount of use of the fund grants at this time, and that any attempt initially to carry out a larger annual program would be subject to several objections:	(1) the additional financial aid from the
federal government would necessarily be applied to less urgent projects, and the value of the projects relative to other types of expenditure would be less; (2) as long as the grade crossing program remains a co-operative one-and we are strongly of the view that it should so remain- an expansion of federal grants without regard to the ability of other parties to finance their share would either cause an unwarranted strain on railway or municipal finances or leave a certain portion of the available grants unused; (3) apart from financial and economic limitations, there are also limitations of skilled labour, engineering personnel, equipment and similar items to be considered. Even on the program which we have suggested, we are not assuming an adequate supply of these factors will always be on hand.
I think that paragraph gives a very convincing reason why a larger sum than $5 million was not recommended by the board. As hon. members know, the bill, in that respect at least, embodies the recommendations of the board itself.
Another point on which I should like to touch, Mr. Chairman, is the concern expressed by the hon. member for Danforth with regard to the provision that if the uncommitted balance in the fund at the end of any year exceeds $2 million, then the appropriation for the ensuing year is to be reduced accordingly. I think if hon. members will examine the report of the board they will find that that provision was suggested by the board so that there would not be an accumulation of uncommitted funds in the

grade crossing fund. I think it will be perfectly obvious to all who think about it for a moment that if there are uncommitted funds in the grade crossing fund it will be because there are no projects before the board which it is willing to approve.
The hon. member for Regina quoted some figures with regard to the number of accidents at protected crossings and contrasted them with the number of accidents at unprotected crossings. From those figures he drew what seemed to be an unwarranted assumption that because the accident rate at protected crossings was greater than at unprotected crossings we should re-examine the whole question and lay greater emphasis on grade separations.
I think the hon. member has failed to realize that one reason why the ratio of accidents at protected crossings is higher than at unprotected crossings is that the volume of traffic is substantially higher and therefore the possibility of accident much greater.

subtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: May I point out to the minister that I mentioned specifically the fact that the accident rate was due to the greater volume of traffic.

subtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Then probably we are in agreement as to the cause, although perhaps not as to the assumption or inference that ought to be drawn from these statistics. At all events I do not think there is any real difference of opinion between the hon. member and me. I think we are probably agreed that at the heavily travelled crossings it is desirable, where possible and where finances permit, to have grade separations rather than automatic or mechanical protection.
At the same time I do not think that we should overlook the fact that protection is highly important. I think the board believes that it is just as important to provide protection at level crossings, particularly where the volume of traffic is not of heavy density, as it is in the case of urban municipality crossings. I suppose that inevitably the provision of flashing lights, bells and short-arm gates will continue to be the basis of any protection program carried out by the board.
I should like to reassure hon. members, particularly those representing rural constituencies, that it is certainly not the intention of the board, if one may judge from what is said in their report, to concentrate their expenditures strictly in the urban areas and overlook the important advantages that would accrue from establishing protective devices at what I might refer to as grade crossings in rural areas.
Railway Act
A good deal of stress has been laid by hon. members on the desirability of embodying in this bill a provision for a penalty for those who disregard signs which are placed by order of the board of transport commissioners.
I should like to repeat what was said by the board because similar representations were made to it during the course of the inquiry. I should like to quote from page 69 of the report as follows:
Other suggestions, more closely allied to motor vehicle operation, including those of an educational nature respecting public observance of grade crossing signs and protective devices, compulsory speed reduction and compulsory stopping of vehicles under certain conditions, and the strict enforcement of prescribed highway safety regulations were placed before us.
These are matters not within the jurisdiction of the board but, nevertheless, they are of interest to the board and might usefully meet with the attention of the provincial committees herein elsewhere suggested, as they constitute a part of the overall problem of highway accidents concerning which there is a rapidly amounting national awareness.
As some hon. members have pointed out, when this bill was before the standing committee, counsel for Canadian National Railways suggested that an amendment be made-I think the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra gave the substance a few moments ago, if not the text, of the proposed amendment-and then suggested to the committee that if there was legislation of this nature it would be possible for the railways to prosecute persons who disregarded protective signs.
I must say that I have not been wholly convinced as to the sincerity of those statements because if there had been a desire on the part of the railways to prosecute offenders there were already several statutes on the books of several of the provinces of Canada under which prosecutions might have been laid. It was not necessary that they should prosecute solely for reckless driving. This afternoon one hon. member referred to the legislation in Saskatchewan and I had occasion the other day to refer to the legislation in Nova Scotia. Section 117 of the motor vehicle act of Nova Scotia reads:
Whenever a person driving a vehicle approaches a highway and railway grade crossing and a clearly visible or positive signal gives warning of the immediate approach of a railway engine, train or car, it shall be an offence for the driver of the vehicle to fail to stop the vehicle before traversing such grade crossing.
There is similar legislation in British Columbia. I think the fact that there is this legislation demonstrates two things. First, that if the railways desire to prosecute there is legislation available in many of the provinces under which action can be taken

Railway Act
and, secondly, the fact that this legislation has been adopted by the provincial legislatures shows that this is a subject which comes properly within the purview of provincial legislation dealing with highways. For these reasons I think the board was quite right in indicating in its report that this was a matter to be dealt with by provincial legislation and not by an amendment to the Railway Act.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra referred to a section of the Railway Act, I think it was section 416. I do not believe that the principle embodied in section 416 is comparable to what we are talking about. The existing provision relates to persons passing on foot across the right of way and I do not think that this is a matter of dealing with the right of way part of the highway. Clearly this is legislation which refers to the movement of vehicles on highways and it should be dealt with by the provinces.
The hon. member for Oxford spoke about a crossing in the town of Ingersoll. Perhaps that case will give me an opportunity to answer another question at the same time. 1 think the situation is simply that the correspondence which the hon. member read emanated, as I understood it, from the Canadian National Railways and representatives of the town of Ingersoll. I would think that the proper course for the town of Ingersoll to follow would be to take up the matter with the board of transport commissioners. I have made inquiry and am informed that it is not the practice of the board to make a mandatory order to force a municipality to carry out works of protection which they are unwilling or unable to do. So that, Mr. Chairman, in the case of Ingersoll, if the town authorities will communicate with the board of transport commissioners, I am sure that any representations they may make will be considered sympathetically by the board.
At the same time I should like to say just this further word. The question has been raised with regard to the constitutionality of the provision under which the board of transport commissioners may assess a portion of the cost of a grade crossing protection or a grade separation project upon a municipal corporation. It seems to me that it should not be overlooked that this is a provision that has long been in the Railway Act and I thought, if I understood the hon. member for Oxford correctly, that it had actually been the subject of a decision by the privy council which settled the question quite positively in affirming that this was legislation competent to the federal parliament. Consequently I do not think we should attach too much importance to the views of those who now seem to have some doubts on the constitutional

aspects, inasmuch as the privy council has already rendered its judgment.
I think there is perhaps one other important subject upon which I should touch, namely the question of the costs of maintenance. I should merely like to remind the committee that the recommendation of the board was that, as to future projects, a contribution towards maintenance costs up to $200 in any one case might be made. As I said earlier, during the discussion of the resolution or on the second reading of this bill, this was the only recommendation of the board which we did not feel we should accept. But as I indicated at the time, and as I think I repeated before the standing committee, if experience shows that we should reconsider this aspect of the question, we shall be glad to do it in the light of the new provisions concerning the grade crossing fund.
I should like to emphasize the fact that it is only a matter of $200. I doubt very much, particularly in the examples which have been cited today, if a contribution of $200, of which the municipal share would probably be proportionately one-half, would determine whether a municipality would or would not accept responsibility to participate in providing protection or grade separation. At all events, Mr. Chairman, I will repeat what I said before. If experience shows that this provision would fill an urgent need, we shall be glad to reconsider our decision not to recommend it to parliament at the present time.
I should also like to emphasize the fact that the principal beneficiaries from this proposal would be the railways. The individual municipality itself would not benefit by any substantial amount. The benefit would accrue principally to the railways. I think hon. members will appreciate that the other provisions of the bill afford much more substantial relief to the railways. I do not think they should complain too strongly that with respect to future projects the costs of maintenance are not going to be absorbed by the grade crossing fund, even with the limitation of $200.
I think the only other point that I should deal with is the question of priorities which was raised by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary. As I understand it, there is no system of priorities. Each of the projects that are submitted to the board is examined on its own merits. Each is approved. There is not a long waiting list which has to be reviewed at the end of the year. The board realizes that the only way in which we can make genuine progress towards the solution of the problem is to deal with meritorious projects as they come before the board and

not to wait in order to establish a long list of priorities either as between one province and another or as between one project and another.
Mr. Chairman, there is only one final word I should like to say and it is this. I do not think anybody believes that, by voting $5 million to the grade crossing fund, we are thereby going to solve the problem of accidents at grade crossings. I think that the trouble can be ended only when the education of the public is complete and when people-drivers in particular-realize the dangers of crossing a railway without taking adequate precautions. The fact that so many accidents take place at protected crossings certainly shows that there is a need for much more care on the part of the drivers than is exercised at the present time. I suppose we shall only solve the problem ultimately when drivers generally have assumed a greater degree of care in driving their cars and when, at the busiest crossings, we are able to construct grade separations instead of protective devices.
After the full discussion we have had on this bill I hope it will now be possible to adopt it so as to enable the board of transport commissioners to make grants from the fund and to start with this larger sum of money towards making greater progress in solving the grade crossing problem.
