that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Canada Elections Act including provision for an increase in the salary of the chief electoral officer.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARY OP CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the resolution, which is very simple, is twofold. In the first place the resolution calls for the putting into effect of the recommendations made by the standing committee on privileges and elections which, through its chairman, tabled a report on the 29th of April. The draft bill attached to the report contains the changes in the act. I might say that none of these changes is of a very serious nature. The committee held quite a number of sittings. Recommendations were made to the committee by different departments of the government, by members of the house and by other organizations.
The second part of the resolution concerns the increase in the salary of the chief electoral officer. The bill to follow the resolution will contain provision for such increase so as to enable the chief electoral officer to receive remuneration comparable to the status of a deputy minister which he holds under the statute.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARY OP CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER, ETC.
speechtext:
In rising to speak on the
resolution I do so with very limited experience of the elections act. However, I had a very enjoyable experience as a member of the standing committee on privileges and elections. I was very much impressed with the conduct and actions of the chief electoral officer. I felt the answers he gave to the

Canada Elections Act
questions asked and the presentation he made before the committee certainly indicated that he was non-partisan in his conduct so far as any matters relating to elections are concerned. With reference to the proposed increase in pay, if the man is worthy of his hire, and I certainly think he is, he is entitled to the increase suggested by the Secretary of State.
I believe the committee might have gone a little further in making recommendations, particularly so since certain sections of our country are becoming more built up and are faced with the problems of increasing population. I have some specific suggestions. The first one is that the hour of closing of the polls might be advanced to seven o'clock instead of six o'clock. I make this suggestion because in the more built-up areas where people live in one area and work in another some miles away they leave before the polls open in the morning and return after they close at night. I fully recognize the act provides that every employee must be given time off to vote by his employer, but I suggest the fact of the matter is that most employees do not take the time. Perhaps they are not aware of the provision in the act. The extension of the voting period by one hour would overcome the difficulty. The problem has already been dealt with by the province of Ontario where the hour of closing of the polls has been extended to seven o'clock to accommodate people in the suburban ridings. One might say that it is a problem of suburbia.
My second suggestion is that the advance poll might embrace a wider group of citizens, and again the province from which I come has already taken action in this regard. Contrary to the suggestions put forward by one of the government members on the committee, I suggest that voting is primarily a right and not a privilege. It may also be a privilege to vote but it goes further than that and is a right. I think the right should be extended to all persons, and if it is necessary for a person to be away from their own district on voting day for some reason I think they should have the right to vote at an advance poll. People could take advantage of the opportunity to vote. There would be no great rush of persons wanting to vote ahead of time but people who are conscientious about their duties as citizens could exercise their franchise. I make this suggestion to the Secretary of State so that an amendment may be incorporated in the act before the next election.
The act provides that there shall be a statutory day of voting, Monday. I think this matter can bear investigation. We wish everyone to have the opportunity to vote.

We want them to be able to consider carefully the candidates for whom they are voting, and we must also recognize that women are taking a more important place in the affairs and life of the country. All of us no doubt have worked on election days and we know what happens when you call for a person to take them to vote and they are in the middle of doing a washing. They rush out, perhaps vote rather hurriedly, and rush back again. By fixing a statutory day we are perhaps losing the vote of some women who are busily occupied on Monday which, after all, is washday. I suggest that the removal of the provision fixing Monday as election day might be considered in order that the act might be more flexible.
Again, the custom is developing throughout the country of people taking long week ends. Maybe they return on Monday morning and they want to go to work immediately. They do not have the opportunity to properly assess the situation on a Monday. If elections were held on some other day than Monday I suggest to the Secretary of State that probably a greater percentage of voters would go to the polls.
I also suggest there should be some provision in the act to prohibit the holding of elections in the months of July and August. Many people are not at home at election time in the holiday months, and it is too much to ask people who work hard 50 weeks of the year to deny themselves the right to their holidays. While the franchise is dear to us, nevertheless it is asking a little too much of people to expect them to return from their holidays to vote. I suggest the Secretary of State might consider that matter with a view to changing the legislation.
I do not know how my next suggestion could be incorporated in our present voting system. The matter would perhaps require considerable study. At the present time representation in the house is not in any way in accordance with the popular vote. In the 1953 election the government members received 2,819,813 votes out of a total of 5,701,963, or less than half the popular vote. The fact that they received less than half the popular vote is not represented in any way by the number of seats they hold in the house. They have a quite extraordinary majority of seats which they won with less than half the popular vote. I am not suggesting the answer. I merely point out the situation to the house and the country as a whole. The fact is that the people who are governing the country and who have such a vast majority of seats actually received less than half of the votes cast by the people

who voted at the last election. I would suggest that to the minister for any consideration he wishes to give it. With these remarks, and with the added support and commendation of the electoral officer I mentioned at the outset, I conclude.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARY OP CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like first of all, Mr. Chairman, to join with the Secretary of State and the hon. member for Peel in the tribute all of us are happy to pay to the fairness and efficiency with which the chief electoral officer, Mr. Nelson Castonguay, carries out his duties. I am sure we all agree with the Secretary of State that, having voiced these tributes so often, it is good to have the opportunity to express these tributes in the more concrete form which has been suggested by the Secretary of State.
As had been pointed out the purpose of this resolution is to forecast the introduction of a bill, which I take it will be substantially along the lines of the draft bill recommended by the committee on privileges and elections. That draft bill can be found in Votes and Proceedings for Friday, April 29,	1955.
Although the draft bill is rather voluminous, containing some 90 pages or more, we all recognize that for the most part it involves technical changes. Indeed, to a large extent they are changes that have been suggested by the chief electoral officer as a result of his experience with the general election of 1953. In so far as there are any changes of substance involved in this proposed legislation, we have the knowledge that they were worked out and agreed to by the members of the standing committee on privileges and elections.
Other members have made or no doubt will make suggestions as to additional improvements which should be made in the Canada Elections Act at this time. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that the time has come when our federal law respecting elections, the Canada Elections Act, should be tightened up with regard to election expenses and particularly with regard to the reporting of election expenses. I am aware of the fact that this subject is touched upon slightly in the draft bill, but only slightly. There is a suggestion in the draft bill that the amount of money a candidate himself may expend in the course of an election, which at the moment is fixed at $1,000, be fixed at a limit of $2,000. This change is to be made in section 62 of the Canada Elections Act.
I regret that, as yet, we have not heard that there is to be any change in section 63 or any of the other sections relating to election expenses and the reporting of those
Canada Elections Act
expenses after the election is over. As hon. members are aware, in 1949 there was before this house a bill which was introduced by the hon. member for Quebec South. This bill dealt with the whole question and suggested, in concrete and specific form, changes that would tighten up the election act with regard to election expenses. As most members are aware, I made a suggestion to him the other day that he might consider reintroducing that bill at this session. I hope he will give serious consideration to that suggestion. The bill was based on the lengthy experience he has had, and it arose out of legislation that was considered at a time when he was a member of the cabinet. It seemed to me that the hon. member for Quebec South had some very useful suggestions in that bill introduced in the first session of 1949.
I would remind the Secretary of State and the members of the house generally, that that bill seemed to meet with general approval in 1949. In fact, it not only passed first reading in the usual perfunctory manner but it passed second reading with just as much speed. There was no discussion at all. After that, it went through the committee of the whole in about a minute or two if one can judge from looking at Hansard. However, for reasons that were not given, it was not proceeded with any further at the 1949 session.
What is the situation at the moment with respect to the reporting of election expenses? The Canada Elections Act. says that all candidates in a federal election must, on their own behalf and through their official agents, report their election expenses. There are forms on which this is to be done, and it is supposed to be done within two months after the candidate in each constituency has been declared elected. Despite that fact I have in my hand sessional paper No. 3-C, which was tabled on Wednesday, January 13, 1954, in reply to certain questions which I placed on the order paper. It indicates that at that date there were 133 candidates in the general election of August 10, 1953, who had not yet filed their election returns as at January 13, 1954.
May I make it clear that these 133 did not include any elected members. It appears that all the members who were elected on August 10, 1953, took the precaution to obey the law and see to it that their election expenses were reported within the proper time. But there were 133 defeated candidates who did not bother to meet that provision; at least they had not done so by January 13, 1954. I find that nothing was done about this illegal practice. I use that word advisedly because, according to one of the sections in

Canada Elections Act
the act, section 63, subsection 8, it is an illegal practice to fail to carry out the requirement that election expense returns be filed.
I notice also that according to a certain subsection of section 81, which can be found on pages 229 and 230 of the green book entitled "General Election Instructions for Returning Officers", there are certain penalties to be applied to those who commit corrupt practices or illegal practices. Let me make it clear that the failure to turn in one's election expense return is not listed as a corrupt practice but rather as an illegal practice. The maximum penalty for an illegal practice, as set out in section 81 is that such person, during the five years next after the date of his being so reported, convicted, ordered or found guilty, shall be incapable of being elected to or of sitting in the House of Commons or of voting at any election of a member of that house or of holding any office in the nomination of the crown or of the governor in council.
Now, it is one of my complaints that although there are these 133 persons who committed an illegal act in that they did not file their expense returns nothing has been done about it. Apparently it is difficult to impose this penalty on them, to deny them the right to run again within five years, or to vote at any election within five years, because certain technicalities have not been carried out. They would have to be reported in a document to Mr. Speaker, and it would have to be indicated that they had been heard on their own behalf; and it would have to be declared that they were persons who should be expressly disqualified, as therein provided.
But it just so happens that, although these 133 persons were not reported directly to Mr. Speaker, in the terms set out in the act, they were reported to the House of Commons in sessional paper 3-C which was tabled on Wednesday, January 13, 1954. And I find that among these 133 persons there are some whose names are known to certain people. For instance, there is a gentleman named Mr. O'Reilly who was the Liberal candidate in Hamilton West. There is Mr. Montgomery who was the Liberal candidate in Lanark. There is the name of Mr. Roland Angers who was the Liberal candidate in Chicoutimi, and that of Mr. Henri Courtemanche who was the Progressive Conservative candidate in Labelle. There is the name of Mr. Eric Wilfred Balcom, not the hon. member for Halifax who sits in this House of Commons, but who, I understand, is a relative of that hon. member, and who was the Liberal candidate in the constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings.

There is the name of Mr. Leonard Francis Hodgson-just to pick a name at random- who was the Social Credit candidate in the constituency of Nanaimo; and there is Mr. Patrick Sheehan O'Dwyer who was the Liberal candidate in Yorkton. There is the name of Mr. George Black, the Progressive candidate in the constituency of Yukon. And there are other names to a total of 133 persons reported to the House of Commons, but not technically reported to Mr. Speaker.
May I say another word about this information that was reported to the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARY OP CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would assist me. The resolution is in very general terms, but I understand the changes have been considered in the committee. I have been leafing through the bill and have not yet found any reference to the matter the hon. member is discussing. I wonder if he would help me in that respect.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARY OP CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER, ETC.
speechtext:
I would be glad to help you, Mr. Chairman, in two ways. First of all I would point out that the hon. member who preceded me was permitted to make suggestions as to changes which should be made at this time in the Canada Elections Act, when it is being amended. Like him, I am making suggestions as to changes which should be made. I think as a matter of fact I am a little closer to the proposed legislation than was the hon. member who preceded me, because there is in the draft bill-which I admit is not before us, but to which reference has been made-at least one change in the matter of election expenses.
I am suggesting that we should act further at this time in the matter of election expenses, and with respect to the reporting of such expenses, so far as our federal legislation is concerned. And if Your Honour is looking for the reference, I suggest that it occurs in the draft bill where reference is made to section 62 of the act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARY OP CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER, ETC.
speechtext: I have noted the clause in the bill, but I find that it deals with the subject of personal expenses of a candidate. It does not deal with the matter of reporting those expenses at some later time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARY OP CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I suggest the expenses of the candidate is one of the items required to be reported. But even if it were not there at all, I suggest that what I am doing is on all fours with what was done by the hon. member who preceded me, and what was done by hon. members who spoke on the last item of legislation before us, when suggestions were made as to other matters that should be dealt with when legislation is before us.

Canada Elections Act
I am urging that at this time the whole matter of the way in which the act spells out how election expenses should be reported should be tightened up. As all members are aware, at the present time even the document to which I have been referring would not come normally to the table of the House of Commons. Under the Canada Elections Act as it now stands we are required merely to report our election expenses to the returning officer in the local constituency. He is required to retain that document in his possession for a period of six months. During that period of six months anyone can go and look at the document simply by paying to the returning officer a fee of 20 cents. At the end of six months he either destroys the document or returns it to the candidate or the official agent.
So far as the law is concerned, election expense returns are never sent to any central place. They are never scrutinized by the chief electoral officer or by any other officer or authority of any kind to determine whether or not the law has been complied with by those filing the returns. I remember one occasion some years ago when I was a defeated candidate going to the returning officer in the constituency and asking to see the return of the hon. gentleman who had defeated me. This was at a time when it cost 10 cents, not 20. I put down the 10 cents and the returning officer got out his receipt book, preparing to make out a receipt. But then he said, "Oh, I am not going to take 10 cents from you. I have been a returning officer for 20 years, and this is the first time anyone has ever asked to see one of these returns".
I recite that incident only to point out how little attention is paid to these election expenses returns, because they simply stay with the local returning officer for a period of six months, at the end of which time they are either returned to the candidate or they are destroyed.
The hon. member for Quebec South made a suggestion in his bill, which came before us in 1949, which was to the effect that these returns should be sent to the chief electoral officer, and that he should have certain authority to check through them and to report to the Speaker of the House of Commons in those instances where anything was irregular or where returns have not been made according to law.
The only reason we have had after the last two elections documents of the kind to which I have been referring is because I happened to put questions on the order paper. As a result of that the chief electoral officer sent out a letter to all the returning officers
asking them to send in such information as they had, so that he could compile this return for the House of Commons.
It is my view that there ought to be some more adequate machinery for checking these returns, to make absolutely sure that the law is complied with right down the line. In recent weeks, and particularly in recent days, there have been many stories and comments in the press about election expenses. Some of these have been on the beam, some have been cynical and some, I think, have been quite unfair, particularly to those who try to obey the law. However, not only do we as members of parliament, and those who ran against us but who were not elected, have a stake in this, but I think the whole country, with its interest in democracy, has a stake in this whole question of election expenses being put on a much more satisfactory basis than they are at the present time.
As Your Honour pointed out a moment ago, a slight change is being made by the bill which it is expected will be founded upon this resolution. But I do not believe that change helps the situation at all. As I understand it at the present time there is no limit on the amount of money that can be spent in an election campaign. The only place where a limit is imposed is that the candidate himself must not, personally, spend directly more than $1,000. But if he wants to contribute $2,000 or $100,000 to the campaign, he can do so. But at the present time any amount that he wants to contribute in excess of $1,000 must be turned over to his official agent, and the official agent must pay the bills. The only change being made is that the amount that the candidate can spend personally is being raised from $1,000 to $2,000. I doubt if many members in this house are interested in that change; we do not spend that kind of money personally. But it raises the whole question, Mr. Chairman, as to whether there should not be some limit on the total amount that can be expended in an election campaign and indeed whether there should not be some restriction on the sources from which contributions could be received.
This latter question has been dealt with in legislation in years gone by, which was abolished. The former question, namely, placing a limit as to the amount that can be expended in any campaign, was the subject matter of Bill No. 7 introduced by the hon. member for Quebec South in 1949.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, all of us have a stake in this question. All candidates at election time, whether they are elected or defeated, have a stake in it. The country as a whole, with its concern for democracy, has

Canada Elections Act a stake in this matter being made more satisfactory than it is at the present time. I urge very strongly that consideration be given to this matter and I would like to see the government introduce legislation along these lines.
Even if the matter was not discussed at the meetings of the committee on privileges and elections, and even if this bill goes through, the government could have that committee meet again at this session or next session to see if something could not be done about this matter, or possibly the hon. member for Quebec South might reintroduce his bill, to give the house a chance to show its support for it, as we did in 1949. In any case, all members will recognize that the time is ripe -indeed I urge that the time has come-for action on this important question of election expenses.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARY OP CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER, ETC.
speechtext:
Before the resolution is carried I have a few remarks to make. The first remark I intend to make is that this bill has been studied by a parliamentary committee of this house, and the members of the committee took care to scrutinize all the proposed amendments contained in the report which was published on April 29 in the Votes and Proceedings.
I was very pleased to listen to the hon. member for Peel. I am sure that he will follow the traditions of his predecessor who who was an excellent member and very popular with his colleagues.
With regard to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I always listen to him with the deepest interest. He made some interesting suggestions today, but as one who has taken part in more elections than he has, and is perhaps not so insistent on the formalities, I shall tell him what is my experience with regard to reports of election expenses. In the first place, he suggested that the amount to be spent in an election should be curtailed or limited. It cannot be done because sometimes election expenses run pretty high, and there is nothing to hide. At the present time the system which has been in force for a long time is excellent. What is being done? There is an election agent who makes his report. There is the member who makes a report of his expenses, and the whole thing is left with the returning officer for six months. Anyone has the opportunity to go to the returning officer, who is well-known in the community, and examine the reports. If they do not, it is because they are satisfied with the way in which the election has been carried on. It is obvious. I will tell that to my hon. friend. Instead of blaming the constituents when nobody goes to
IMr. Knowles.]

the returning officer to check the report, he should realize that it is because everybody in the constituency is satisfied with the way in which the election has been carried on by the candidate. This is my experience; not only my experience but also that of my opponents. I do not know where they got their funds. One made a report, the other one did not. Where did he get his funds? I do not know. I won the election. I did not bother about the poor fellow; I left him to cry about his defeat.
We must be generous in such circumstances. I made my report. The report was published in the press, according to law, and it was left with the returning officer for six months. One of my opponents made a report which I looked at, but which I did not check. The other one did not make a report. If I had complained about it to the returning officer everybody would have thought me mean. They would have said, he has won his election and he is making a martyr of the poor fellow who was defeated. I submit these considerations to my hon. friend. He will understand them very well.
I tell him that even if quite a lot of money was spent on an election the election may have been conducted honestly. For instance, take loud speakers. How much do they cost? They cost on an average $750 for an election. It is an honest expenditure, but it runs pretty high. The cost of radio is pretty high. It is $15 for 15 minutes at the smallest stations. In larger stations it may run up to $60 for a quarter of an hour. It is a lot of money. Then there is the literature. There is no frank during an election. You have to pay for the stamps; you have to pay for the errands; you have to pay for all of that. It is all legitimate expenditures.
I am greatly surprised that the committee has not authorized the candidates to rent cars on election day. There would be nothing immoral or unethical in sending a car for somebody or paying for it. At the present time we have to beg our friends for cars or ask them to pay for a taxi driver. It makes no sense. If the friends of a candidate contribute toward his election there is no reason why he should not hire cars on election day to make it easier for the electors. There is nothing wrong in it. In my experience it is just to be nice, because very often when a taxi is sent to bring someone to vote and the elector asks who is sending the taxi and you say "so and so", sometimes he laughs and votes for the other side. Who can control the vote of one who goes to the polling booth in a limousine or in a Ford car? Sometimes electors want to ride in a nice car. I think that is only proper because that is the day when they are masters of the situation. It

is only natural that they should want to be well taken care of. Why should we be hypocrites and say that no member pays anything to provide driving accommodation so that the electors may vote? There is nothing wrong in that. It is not purchasing votes; it is not infringing upon their liberties; it is simply giving them a chance to observe the law with the least effort. I do not see anything wrong about it and I am sorry the law does not take this into consideration. There is something much more serious than what the hon. gentleman has said, and I say that in the friendliest way.
As a rule elections are carried on honestly. I believe that all members of parliament representing all groups have been elected honestly according to the constitution and the practices of the country which have existed for so long. I say that, not only about hon. members on this side of the house but about all my colleagues.
What I think is more important is the way in which the right to vote is granted and to whom. The committee did an excellent job when it refused to accept the proposal by an employee of the Department of External Affairs that all the employees of that department located outside of Canada should have the right to vote. The right to vote is important and in this I am in accord with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that it should be given only to those who will use that right within the boundaries of the country.
I stated before the committee that the right to vote which was given to our soldiers was a privilege. That right which was given to members of the forces stationed outside of Canada was something out of the ordinary, it was a tremendous privilege. Why should we grant it to civil servants or to the wives of soldiers stationed outside of Canada? It is enough to give it to the soldiers without giving it to their wives, who most of the time know nothing about the business of the country.
They could be asked, who is the Prime Minister of Canada, who is the Leader of the Opposition, who is the Minister of National Defence and they would be unable to answer. Yet they are to be qualified to vote. Many of them have never been in Canada and yet they would be qualified to express their opinions about Tom who is a Liberal candidate, Jim who is a Conservative candidate, Paul who is a C.C.F. candidate, and another gentleman who is a Social Crediter.
Canada Elections Act
What do they know about it? Simply because this tremendous privilege is given to members of our armed forces does not mean that the same privilege should be given to their wives who are not familiar with Canadian politics. There should be an end to that. The committee did a splendid thing when it refused the suggestion of the representative of the Department of External Affairs to grant the same right to members of that department who were stationed outside of Canada.
When I saw the judge advocate general and this gentleman from the Department of External Affairs appear before the committee I felt that what they wanted was a Cook's tour around the world to visit all places where soldiers were stationed or where members of that department were to be found. I was surprised to hear from the chief electoral officer that only one-third of the soldiers actually vote. Why give the vote to their wives? The committee said "no" when the gentleman from the Department of External Affairs made his fine suggestion.
What scandalized me was that when I told him he was not well enough prepared to appear before the committee one of the members of the committee was shocked. He could not understand that I should say that a civil servant was not well enough prepared to appear before the committee and give the information asked for. He had worked on this proposal for two years but he was unsuccessful and he will not have his Cook's tour. But the judge advocate general will have his Cook's tour as the opportunity to vote is to be given to the wives of soldiers. In the one case it was refused, in the other case it was granted. I do not see why the judge advocate general should be granted this Cook's tour.
The best way to have an honest election is to teach people how to vote. The proportion of those who vote will then be much larger. There are some reasons why people do not vote. They may be sick, they may have to be away. It is better to have a smaller number of voters who vote right in Canada than to have a larger number who vote by power of attorney or by correspondence. How can it be checked?
These are considerations that I leave with the committee of the whole. I congratulate the minister upon the way he left the committee free to decide by itself what it thought was the best thing to do. I join with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in what he said about Mr. Oastonguay. He was most informative when before the committee

Canada Elections Act
and was always ready to answer. He deserves this increase in salary which is being provided.
I can remember when his father received only $4,000 for doing all this work at a time when a son of a former prime minister received $10,000 for doing nothing. I was the one who protested and I succeeded in having the salary of the father increased. I am glad that the son is following in the traditions of his father.
I can tell my hon. friend that from my long experience I can say that I have not seen anything wrong in the way elections have been carried out, and hon. members who sit here as well as those who sat in the
ten previous parliaments have nothing to be ashamed of for having been elected to the parliament of Canada.
Progress reported.
